questions.prompt: Single-cell RNA-seq flags a candidate marker gene for a colon-innervating [[DRG]] subtype you want to silence. Put the path from that cluster to a functional test in order.
items: Confirm the marker is expressed in real DRG neurons with [[RNAscope]]
Get or make a [[Cre]] line driven by that marker gene
Give the actuator ([[DCZ]]) with the right controls
Read out behavior/physiology and confirm the neurons were silenced
questions.explanation: A cluster is a hypothesis (C12): RNAscope grounds it in tissue (C8), a Cre line gives genetic access (C2/C3), a Cre-dependent AAV restricts the tool to those cells (C4), and only then does an actuator + readout test function (C5). Skipping validation or genetic access is where projects go wrong.

questions.prompt: A colon afferent stops responding to balloon distension after a genetic manipulation, yet still responds normally to capsaicin. Which single change best fits?
options: Loss of [[Piezo2]], the channel its endings use to sense stretch
Loss of [[TRPV1]], the receptor that its endings use to detect stretch
Demyelination of the afferent, which removes its response to stretch
An [[hM4Di]] DREADD was expressed and is now silencing the whole neuron
questions.explanation: Distension is a mechanical stimulus (D5) transduced by Piezo2 (A4); capsaicin acts through TRPV1 (A3). A still-normal capsaicin response means the neuron is alive and TRPV1 works, so the defect is mechanical — Piezo2. TRPV1 loss would kill the capsaicin response; demyelination slows conduction rather than removing one stimulus; a silencing DREADD would blunt both responses.

questions.prompt: Your [[antibody]] stain and your [[RNAscope]] both light up the same neurons for marker X, but a reviewer still doubts the X protein is really there. What is the strongest single addition?
options: Show the antibody signal disappears in tissue from a marker-X knockout
Add a secondary-only slide to rule out background from the secondary
Repeat the RNAscope with more probe pairs for a brighter signal
Re-image the same slide on a confocal at higher magnification
questions.explanation: mRNA and protein agreeing is independent support, but the two can diverge (C8-L1), so it isn't proof of the protein. The knockout is the clincher (C7): real signal vanishes without the target. A secondary-only control guards against a different error (false positives from the secondary); more probes and higher magnification address brightness and resolution, not specificity.

questions.prompt: Two DRG afferents carry the same stimulus, but one's signal reaches the cord much sooner. Which property best explains the faster one?
options: A larger diameter with a [[myelination|myelinated]] axon
A more negative resting membrane potential at the ending
A larger number of [[TRPV1]] channels packed at its ending
A smaller diameter, which lowers its internal resistance
questions.explanation: Conduction velocity rises with diameter and myelination (D4) — the Aβ-vs-C logic (A5). Resting potential and ending TRPV1 density affect excitability and sensing, not how fast a spike travels. And smaller diameter raises, not lowers, internal resistance, so it conducts slower.

questions.setup: You need to silence only pancreas-innervating sensory neurons, in an adult mouse, without hitting the same neuron type in other organs and without acting from birth.
questions.prompt: Which approach fits all three constraints?
options: Retrograde [[Cre]] from the pancreas, a Cre-dependent [[hM4Di]] AAV, and [[DCZ]] in adulthood
A germline [[Nav1.8]]-Cre mouse crossed to a floxed hM4Di allele, given DCZ in adulthood
A pancreatic injection of a no-Cre [[hM3Dq]] AAV, then activation with [[CNO]] in adulthood
Optogenetic silencing through an optic fiber placed over the entire DRG in an adult mouse
questions.reveal: Retrograde Cre delivered from the organ restricts targeting by *projection* (pancreas), the Cre-dependent AAV restricts the tool to those cells, and giving the actuator in adulthood avoids developmental effects (C4/C5) — the colon paper's playbook aimed at the pancreas. A germline Nav1.8-Cre hits that type body-wide from birth; a no-Cre hM3Dq *activates* (and isn't cell-type restricted); optogenetics needs light delivery and over the whole DRG isn't specific.

questions.prompt: The vagal 'inflammatory reflex' and a visceral pain reflex are both [[reflex arc|reflex arcs]]. What do their afferent limbs have in common?
options: Both are sensory neurons sensing the body's internal state ([[interoception]])
Both are motor neurons that drive an effector organ to make the response
Both are [[microglia]] detecting tissue damage from inside the central nervous system
Both run only in the [[vagus]] nerve, never through any spinal DRG neurons
questions.explanation: The afferent limb of any reflex arc is sensory (D8), and for the viscera that sensing is interoception (D5). Motor neurons are the efferent limb; microglia aren't the afferent limb of these arcs; and both vagal (nodose) and spinal (DRG) afferents serve the viscera — the DRG side is exactly the lab's focus.

questions.prompt: A [[TRPV1]]-[[Cre]] reporter line marks *more* adult [[DRG]] neurons than currently express TRPV1. Why?
options: Trpv1-Cre permanently tags any cell that expressed Trpv1 in development, even if it later stops
The reporter leaks sideways into neighboring cells that never once expressed Trpv1 themselves
TRPV1 protein simply degrades far faster than the long-lived reporter protein ever does
Adult neurons keep making fresh TRPV1 that the antibody is simply unable to detect
questions.explanation: Cre recombines the reporter in any lineage cell that ever turned on Trpv1; some downregulate TRPV1 in adulthood but keep the reporter, so reporter+ exceeds TRPV1+ now. It's a lineage trace, not a snapshot.

visual.alt: Developing DRG neurons expressing Trpv1 are permanently tagged by Trpv1-Cre; in the adult some no longer make TRPV1 but keep the reporter, so reporter-positive cells outnumber TRPV1-positive ones.

questions.prompt: In a calcium-imaging run you test [[capsaicin]] on DRG neurons, then finish with a high-KCl pulse. What is the KCl pulse for?
options: A positive control that silent cells were alive and excitable, not dead
A negative control for background fluorescence coming off the dish
To wash the capsaicin back off the cells before imaging ends
To convert the touch neurons into capsaicin-sensitive ones first
questions.explanation: KCl depolarizes any healthy neuron, so a cell silent to capsaicin but responsive to KCl is genuinely capsaicin-insensitive, not dead. A cell silent to both is excluded as unhealthy.

questions.prompt: [[Piezo2]] is the main touch-transduction channel in skin. What does its role in the gut tell you?
options: The same mechanical channel also transduces stretch of the visceral wall
Gut sensation must therefore be entirely chemical, never mechanical
The channel switches over to sensing temperature once it is in the gut
The gut uses Piezo2 only for pain, and never for normal filling
questions.explanation: Piezo2 is a mechanically-activated channel used for touch in skin and for wall stretch in the viscera — one transducer, two jobs, which is why deleting it blunts both.

questions.prompt: A marker gene labels a colon [[DRG]] subtype but is *also* on enteric and sympathetic neurons. How do you label only the DRG cells?
options: Intersect two drivers, so only cells with both the marker and a DRG-specific feature are caught
Use a single Cre line for the marker and simply accept the extra enteric and sympathetic cells
Raise an antibody to the marker protein and image the entire gut wall all at once under one scope
Switch to a much stronger promoter so the DRG cells outshine all of the rest
questions.explanation: Intersectional genetics requires two coincident features, so only the DRG cells that carry both the marker and the DRG-defining driver are captured — the logic the colon paper used.

questions.prompt: You want to label only sensory neurons innervating the pancreas, not those of other organs. Which approach fits?
options: Inject a retrograde virus into the pancreas; only its own projecting neurons take it up
Inject an anterograde virus into the DRG and wait for label to reach the pancreas
Give a systemic dye through the blood and let it spread through the entire body evenly
Use a germline reporter that labels every sensory neuron in the whole body at once
questions.explanation: A retrograde virus placed in the organ is taken up by the terminals that project there, so expression is restricted to that organ's afferents — targeting by projection.

questions.prompt: [[hM3Dq]] excites a neuron and [[hM4Di]] silences it. In membrane terms, what differs when the actuator binds?
options: hM3Dq drives depolarization toward threshold; hM4Di hyperpolarizes away from it
Both receptors depolarize the cell, but hM4Di just does it more slowly over time
hM3Dq removes the resting potential while hM4Di then restores it again afterward
hM4Di speeds up axonal conduction while hM3Dq slows the conduction down instead
questions.explanation: Excitatory DREADDs push the membrane toward threshold (more likely to fire); inhibitory DREADDs hyperpolarize it (less likely). It's about membrane potential relative to threshold, not conduction speed.

questions.prompt: When capsaicin opens [[TRPV1]] at rest, Na⁺ rushes *into* the neuron. Why that direction?
options: At rest both the gradient and the voltage push Na⁺ inward — a large inward driving force
An open channel always moves its ions out of the cell first before ever letting any in
TRPV1 actively pumps Na⁺ inward using ATP energy, the way an ion pump would
Sodium is simply repelled by the cell's positively charged interior and forced in
questions.explanation: At the resting potential, Na⁺ is far from its equilibrium, so both chemistry and voltage drive it inward through any open channel. TRPV1 is a passive channel, not a pump.

questions.prompt: A body region has many neurons, each with a tiny [[receptive field]]. In coding terms, what does that give?
options: Fine spatial acuity, close to a labeled-line map of stimulus location
Coarse localization overall, but with a much faster conduction speed
Pure rate coding, carrying no spatial information about location at all
Nearly identical responses from every neuron across the whole region
questions.explanation: Small, dense receptive fields let the brain pinpoint where a stimulus is — a near labeled-line map of space. Field size sets acuity, not conduction speed.

questions.prompt: Why is visceral pain vague and hard to place, compared with a sharp skin pinprick?
options: Few afferents with large receptive fields give the brain only a coarse spatial map
The viscera contain no sensory neurons, so the brain simply guesses
Visceral signals travel to the brain far more slowly than skin signals do
Organ pain is processed only in the spinal cord, and never in the brain
questions.explanation: Sparse innervation with large fields means the brain gets 'something's wrong in there' but not precisely where — the opposite of the skin's dense, fine-grained map.

questions.prompt: A neuron with its cell body in the [[DRG]] innervates the gut. Is it an autonomic motor neuron?
options: No — it's a sensory afferent; autonomic motor is a separate efferent system
Yes — any neuron that reaches the gut is by definition an autonomic one
Yes — DRG neurons are the motor side of the parasympathetic nervous system
No — it must instead be a somatic motor neuron projecting to skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: DRG neurons are sensory afferents (interoceptive here). 'Autonomic' is a motor/efferent division — a different axis from 'sensory vs motor', a classic mix-up.

questions.prompt: You cut the dorsal root of a spinal nerve, sparing the ventral root. What is lost?
options: That root's sensory input, while motor output via the ventral root is spared
That root's motor output, while sensory input through the ventral root is spared
Both sensation and movement, since the two roots carry identical fibers
Nothing at all, because the signals simply reroute through the opposite side
questions.explanation: The dorsal root is sensory, the ventral root motor — the classic demonstration that the roots are functionally separate (overlap from neighboring roots can soften the sensory loss).

questions.setup: You cross a subtype-marker [[Cre]] line to a floxed-STOP reporter.
questions.prompt: Which cells end up labeled?
options: Cells that have expressed the marker, where Cre excised the stop cassette
Every neuron in the animal, whether or not it ever expressed the marker
Only the cells that happen to be dividing at the time of the cross
No cells at all, since Cre and the reporter must be injected separately
questions.reveal: Cre is made only where the marker's promoter is active; it removes the stop, switching on the reporter in exactly those cells (and their lineage). That's how a line marks a defined subtype.

questions.prompt: You want only a few neurons labeled so single axons can be traced. What's the trick with [[CreER]]?
options: Give a low dose of tamoxifen, so Cre activates in only a sparse subset of cells
Give a high dose of tamoxifen, so that every eligible cell lights up at once
Skip the tamoxifen entirely and let CreER recombine all on its own anyway
Give the tamoxifen later, in adulthood, which by itself labels only a few cells
questions.explanation: CreER only recombines when tamoxifen is present, and a low dose catches only a fraction of eligible cells — sparse labeling that lets you resolve single arbors.

questions.prompt: A demyelinating condition strips [[myelin]] from a sensory nerve. What happens to its signals?
options: Conduction slows or blocks, because fast [[saltatory conduction]] is lost
Conduction speeds up, since the myelin had been slowing the axon
The neuron's resting potential collapses all the way to zero
Conduction speed is unchanged, since speed is set by axon diameter alone
questions.explanation: Myelin enables saltatory conduction; without it the spike must creep along bare membrane or fails between nodes, so conduction slows or blocks.

questions.prompt: To show two marker genes define one [[DRG]] subtype, what must [[RNAscope]] reveal?
options: Both probe signals inside the very same cells, not merely in the same region
The two probes landing in separate, neighboring populations of cells instead
A much brighter signal for one of the two probes than for the other one
Both markers detected together in a bulk lysate of the whole ganglion
questions.explanation: Co-expression means both colors in the same DAPI-bounded cell. Signals in neighboring cells would mean separate populations; a bulk lysate loses the single-cell resolution entirely.

questions.prompt: You have a new anti-[[TRPV1]] antibody. What most strongly shows it's specific?
options: The staining disappears in knockout tissue that lacks the target protein
The staining looks bright and clean across normal wild-type tissue
The antibody also produces a single band on a western blot
The staining falls exactly where you had expected the target to be
questions.explanation: Specific signal must vanish without the target: a knockout is the clincher. A pretty wild-type stain, a band, or matching your expectation can all occur with an off-target antibody.

questions.prompt: During inflammation, [[cytokine|cytokines]] act on nociceptor endings. What's a direct effect on sensation?
options: They lower the nociceptors' threshold, so milder stimuli now cause pain
They convert the nociceptors into fast, low-threshold touch fibers
They act in the spinal cord instead, leaving the endings themselves unchanged
They raise the threshold, making the inflamed area go numb
questions.explanation: Inflammatory mediators sensitize the ending by lowering its threshold (peripheral sensitization), so normally innocuous stimuli now fire it — the cytokine link between immunity and pain.

questions.prompt: After an injury, gentle touch becomes painful ([[allodynia]]). Which best explains it?
options: Central sensitization: dorsal-horn gain rises, so touch input is read as pain
The touch fibers themselves have physically turned into pain-sensing nociceptors
Peripheral sensitization alone: the touch endings themselves now have a lower threshold
The area is swollen, so ordinary touch presses harder on the nerve endings
questions.explanation: Touch-evoked pain points to raised gain in the dorsal horn (central sensitization), where even Aβ touch input is read as painful — a central change, not a conversion of fiber types.

questions.prompt: You want to watch [[microglia]] extend and retract processes deep in a living brain. Which method fits?
options: Two-photon microscopy through a cranial window
Confocal microscopy, which gives the sharpest single-plane images
A western blot run for a single microglia-specific marker protein
Bulk RNA-seq of the whole dissected brain at one single time point
questions.explanation: Live, deep, dynamic imaging calls for two-photon. Confocal is sharp but can't reach far into living tissue; a blot and bulk-seq lose both the live dynamics and the single-cell spatial detail.

questions.prompt: You want to know *which* cells in inflamed tissue transcribe the cytokine Il6. Best method?
options: [[RNAscope]] for Il6 mRNA, read per cell against [[DAPI]]
A western blot of the inflamed tissue, probed for IL-6
An ELISA for IL-6 run on the whole tissue homogenate
Bulk RNA-seq of the inflamed tissue, sequenced deeply
questions.explanation: Only in-situ detection assigns the signal to particular cells. A blot and ELISA quantify amount; bulk-seq averages over the population, so none say which cells are the source.

questions.prompt: A one-sided cord lesion gives pain/temp loss on the opposite side but fine-touch loss on the same side below it. Why the split?
options: Pain/temp crosses low in the cord; fine touch crosses higher, in the brainstem
Fine touch crosses low in the cord; pain/temp crosses higher, in the brainstem
Both pathways cross in the cord, so one side should lose both kinds of sensation
Neither pathway crosses in the cord, so all the loss should be on the lesioned side
questions.explanation: The spinothalamic tract crosses near entry in the cord, while the dorsal-column pathway crosses up in the brainstem — so one lesion gives contralateral pain/temp but ipsilateral touch.

questions.prompt: A gut afferent ends below the epithelium, not in the lumen, yet reports luminal chemistry. How?
options: Enterochromaffin cells sample the lumen and signal to it using serotonin
The afferent pushes a branch directly into the lumen to taste it on its own
The chemicals diffuse across the epithelium and bind receptors on the ending itself
Enteric neurons in the myenteric plexus sample the lumen and pass the signal on
questions.explanation: Lumen-facing EC cells are the transducer: they sense chemistry and release serotonin onto the nearby afferent — sensing by relay, not direct contact.

questions.setup: Colon afferents come in low-, mid-, and high-threshold subtypes, and you silence only the high-threshold ones with a [[DREADD]].
questions.prompt: What do you predict?
options: Blunted responses to strong, noxious distension; gentle filling still sensed
Loss of all colon sensation at once, the gentle and the strong alike
Stronger pain from gentle, normal filling of the colon than before
Noxious distension still reported, since the low-threshold units cover that range too
questions.reveal: High-threshold units carry the noxious end of the range, so silencing them should spare gentle-filling sensation while blunting responses to harmful distension — a subtype-specific prediction.

questions.prompt: A [[UMAP]] shows a tidy cluster you think is a new DRG subtype. What actually confirms it's a real cell type?
options: Finding its marker gene expressed in real neurons in the tissue
The cluster sitting far away from the others on the plot
The cluster being by far the largest one on the UMAP
The whole plot looking clean, with well-separated blobs
questions.explanation: A cluster is a hypothesis; grounding its marker in tissue (e.g. by RNAscope) is what makes it a real cell type. UMAP distance, cluster size, and tidy blobs are not evidence on their own.
